docs.title: Ethical Hacking
docs.text: Interactive notes · CEH-aligned

docs.title: Attack it. Defend it. Report it.
docs.text:
A CEH-aligned introduction to ethical hacking — learn to scan, test, exploit, and secure systems, and to see every attack from both the attacker's and the defender's side.

12 weeks · 6 modules CEH exam-aligned Interactive notes + video Open-access readings — $0

docs.title: About this course
docs.text: Students scan, test, hack, and secure systems, implement perimeter defenses, and attack and defend virtual networks. Coverage includes intrusion detection, social engineering, footprinting, DoS attacks, buffer overflows, SQL injection, privilege escalation, trojans, backdoors, and wireless hacking, with emphasis on legal and ethical guidelines. The course prepares students for the Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH) exam.

docs.title: Course modules
docs.text: The course is organized into six modules across 12 weeks, following the attacker's kill chain. Each module groups one or more weeks; every week is an interactive notes page tied to its kill-chain phase and CEH topic.

docs.text:
The rules before the tools — ethics, authorization, and the five-phase methodology that frames everything.

Week Topic Week 1 Ethics, Law & Methodology

Week Topic Week 2 Reconnaissance & Footprinting Week 3 Scanning & Enumeration

docs.text:
Listen on the wire and slip past defenses — then the cryptography that protects data and how it fails.

Week Topic Week 4 Network Hacking & Sniffing Week 5 Cryptography — PKI, certificates, attacks

docs.text:
Break into Windows and Linux hosts, then understand the malware, DoS, and session hijacking that follow.

Week Topic Week 6 System Attacks — Windows/Linux Week 7 Trojans, Malware & DoS

docs.text:
Exploit people and the web — social engineering, web-server and web-app attacks, and a SQL-injection deep dive.

Week Topic Week 8 Social Engineering Week 9 Web Attacks I — servers & apps Week 10 Web Attacks II — SQL Injection

docs.text:
Attacks that travel through the air, then a full penetration-test methodology and professional reporting.

Week Topic Week 11 Wireless Hacking (WEP/WPA) Week 12 Penetration Testing

docs.title: What you'll be able to do
docs.text:
By the end of the course you will be able to demonstrate the ability to attack and defend a network — the core learning outcome — and you'll be prepared for the Certified Ethical Hacker (CEH) exam. Concretely, you'll be able to:

  • Conduct reconnaissance and map a target's attack surface.
  • Scan and enumerate hosts, services, and vulnerabilities.
  • Exploit systems and web applications safely and legally.
  • Recognize and reason about malware, DoS, and social-engineering attacks.
  • Apply cryptographic concepts and evade basic network defenses.
  • Plan a penetration test and communicate findings clearly.

docs.title: How this site works
docs.text:
Interactive lecture notes

These pages are the interactive notes that accompany the course videos — concept explanations, the kill-chain framing, ATT&CK tags, and a Defender's view on every topic. Everything else for the course — videos, schedule, and graded work — lives in Canvas.

  • Readings are all free and open-access — NIST, OWASP, the official Nmap book, Crypto 101, Metasploit Unleashed, and more. See the Free Resource Library.
  • Ethics and law run through the whole course, anchored by Alana Maurushat's open-access Ethical Hacking.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• New to the toolset? Skim Kali Linux Revealed before Module 2.

Authorization first

Everything in this course is practiced only on systems you have explicit written permission to test. Unauthorized access to computer systems is a crime — the legal boundaries are covered in Week 1.

docs.title: Week 1 · Ethics, Law & Methodology
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 1 · Ethics, Law & Methodology
docs.text:
🧭 Frames the whole course

What this page covers

  • What ethical hacking is — and the legal line that defines it
  • Authorization, scope, and rules of engagement
  • The five-phase kill chain we'll follow all term
  • MITRE ATT&CK as the shared technique vocabulary
  • How to read the Defender's view panels on every page

docs.title: 1. What is ethical hacking?
docs.text: An ethical hacker uses the same tools and techniques as an attacker — but with written permission and for defense. White, grey, and black hats differ not in skill but in authorization and intent. The whole point of this course: think like an attacker so you can defend like a professional.

docs.title: 2. The legal frame
docs.text: What separates a penetration test from a crime is authorization. Before any testing: a signed scope, rules of engagement, and often a non-disclosure agreement. Unauthorized access is a crime under laws like the U.S. CFAA and state statutes. When in doubt, stop and confirm scope.

docs.title: 3. The five-phase kill chain
docs.text:
Every attack in this course — and most real breaches — follows the same arc. We'll return to this diagram all term: each week lives on one of these phases. Click a phase to see what it means and which weeks cover it.

1 · Reconnaissance Profile the target 2 · Scanning Find what's reachable 3 · Gaining Access Exploit & foothold 4 · Maintaining Persistence & C2 5 · Covering Tracks Evade & clean up

↑ Click any phase to see what it covers

1 · Reconnaissance

Gather information about the target without (or before) touching it directly: footprinting, OSINT, WHOIS, and DNS. The output is a target profile that drives everything else.

Covered in: Week 2 · ATT&CK tactic: Reconnaissance (TA0043) 2 · Scanning & Enumeration

Actively probe the target to find live hosts, open ports, services, and versions — then enumerate those services for users, shares, and configuration.

Covered in: Week 3 (and network sniffing, Week 4) · ATT&CK tactic: Discovery (TA0007) 3 · Gaining Access

Exploit a vulnerability to get code execution — on a system, a web app, a wireless network, or a person. This is the foothold.

Covered in: Weeks 6 (systems), 8 (social engineering), 9–10 (web), 11 (wireless) · ATT&CK tactics: Initial Access (TA0001), Execution (TA0002) 4 · Maintaining Access

Keep the foothold alive: backdoors, trojans/RATs, and command-and-control. Also where denial-of-service and session hijacking live.

Covered in: Week 7 · ATT&CK tactics: Persistence (TA0003), Command & Control (TA0011) 5 · Covering Tracks

Evade detection and hide the intrusion — log tampering, timestomping, and anti-forensics. For the defender, this is where good logging and a pen-test report matter most.

Covered in: Week 12 (methodology & reporting) · ATT&CK tactic: Defense Evasion (TA0005)

docs.title: 4. ATT&CK — the shared vocabulary
docs.text:
Throughout the course, each week is tagged with the MITRE ATT&CK techniques it covers — the same technique IDs used by every SOC and threat-intel team in industry. You'll see a tag strip like this near the top of each page:

ATT&CK TA0043 Recon TA0007 Discovery TA0001 Initial Access

Clicking a tag opens its definition on the MITRE ATT&CK site.

docs.title: 5. The Defender's view
docs.text:
Every attack leaves a trace. On each week's page you'll find a blue Defender's view panel showing how that week's technique looks from the SOC seat — the logs, signatures, or telemetry that reveal it, and the one control that best stops it:

Defender's view — example

Reconnaissance is noisy but easy to dismiss as background internet traffic. A defender watches for directionality and pattern: a single source touching many ports or many URLs in seconds, often with a scanner user-agent. The best control isn't detection — it's reducing what's exposed in the first place.

docs.text:

docs.title: Week 2 · Reconnaissance & Footprinting
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 2 · Reconnaissance & Footprinting
docs.text:
🧭 Kill chain · Phase 1 — Reconnaissance

ATT&CK T1595 Active Scanning T1590 Victim Network Info T1589 Victim Identity Info

What this page covers

  • Passive vs. active reconnaissance
  • WHOIS, DNS, and subdomain discovery
  • OSINT techniques and search operators
  • How a footprint feeds everything that follows

docs.title: 1. Passive vs. active recon
docs.text: Passive recon uses public information and never touches the target directly — it's stealthy and low-risk. Active recon interacts with the target and starts to carry legal weight. You always start passive.

docs.title: 2. WHOIS & DNS
docs.text: Registrars, name servers, and DNS records reveal domains, IP ranges, mail servers, and often subdomains. Certificate-transparency logs are a goldmine for discovering hosts an organization didn't mean to expose.

docs.title: 3. OSINT techniques
docs.text:
Click each to expand.

🔎 Search operators (dorking)

Targeted queries (site:, filetype:, intitle:) surface exposed documents, admin panels, and credentials in public search indexes.

🧾 Metadata & documents

Office/PDF metadata leaks usernames, software versions, and internal paths. Tools like exiftool extract it.

👥 People & tech stack

Job posts, LinkedIn, and GitHub reveal the technologies in use and the people to target for social engineering (Week 8).

docs.title: 4. The footprint
docs.text: The output of this week is a target profile: domains, hosts, emails, technologies, and exposed services. That profile drives your scanning (Week 3) and your social-engineering pretexts (Week 8).

docs.title: Defender's view
docs.text:
How this looks from the SOC seat

Passive recon is essentially invisible — it happens on third-party infrastructure the defender doesn't control. Active footprinting (DNS brute force, subdomain enumeration) can show as spikes in NXDOMAIN responses or automated request patterns.

Best control: you can't detect passive OSINT, so minimize the footprint — reduce metadata leakage, lock down DNS zone transfers, and monitor certificate-transparency logs for shadow assets you didn't know were public.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• NIST SP 800-115 §4 (review & target identification). Free PDF
  • OSINT Framework. osintframework.com
  • MITRE ATT&CK — Reconnaissance (TA0043). attack.mitre.org

docs.title: Week 3 · Scanning & Enumeration
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 3 · Scanning & Enumeration
docs.text:
🧭 Kill chain · Phase 2 — Scanning

ATT&CK T1595 Active Scanning T1046 Service Discovery T1018 Remote System Discovery

What this page covers

  • The main scan types and when to use each
  • Nmap for host discovery, service/OS detection, and scripting
  • Turning open ports into real intel through enumeration
  • How scanning looks from the defender's side

docs.title: 1. Why scan?
docs.text:
Reconnaissance told you who the target is. Scanning tells you what's reachable — which hosts are up, which ports are open, and what's listening. It's the bridge between "here's a domain" and "here's an exploitable service."

Passive recon (Week 2) Active scanning (this week) 🕵️ No packets to the target 📡 You send probes to the target Public data, OSINT, WHOIS/DNS Live host & port discovery Stealthy, low legal risk Noisy — authorization required

docs.title: 2. Scan types
docs.text:
• TCP connect scan — completes the full handshake. Reliable, but loud and logged.
  • SYN ("half-open") scan — sends SYN, never finishes. Faster and quieter.
  • UDP scan — for DNS, SNMP, DHCP. Slower and trickier to read.

Every port comes back as open, closed, or filtered (a firewall is dropping the probe).

docs.title: 3. Nmap in depth
docs.text:
Click each technique to expand.

🔎 Host discovery — who's alive? 

nmap -sn 10.0.0.0/24      # ping sweep, no port scan
Finds live hosts before you spend time scanning ports.

🏷️ Service & version detection 

nmap -sV -p- 10.0.0.5     # all ports, identify service versions
Turns "port 22 open" into "OpenSSH 8.9 — here's the exact version."

🖐️ OS fingerprint + default scripts 
nmap -O -sC 10.0.0.5      # OS guess + safe NSE scripts

docs.title: 4. Enumeration
docs.text:
Scanning finds the door; enumeration reads the nameplate. Once a service is found, you pull details out of it:

  • SMB — shares, users, domains
  • SNMP — device config (watch for the public community string)
  • SMTP — valid usernames via VRFY/RCPT

The goal: convert "a port is open" into "here's the version, the users, and the shares."

docs.title: Defender's view
docs.text:
How this looks from the SOC seat

A ping sweep and a full port scan generate hundreds of connection attempts in seconds — high-signal, but easy to bury in internet background noise. Useful detection looks for one source touching many ports/hosts in a short window, often with a scanner user-agent on web ports.

index=web_logs status=404 (useragent="*nmap*" OR useragent="*gobuster*")
| stats count by clientip | where count > 50

Best control: you can't stop scanning, so reduce the attack surface — close unused ports, put management services behind a VPN, and rate-limit at the edge.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Nmap Network Scanning (official book) — Host Discovery & Port Scanning. nmap.org/book
  • NIST SP 800-115 §4.2–4.3. Free PDF

docs.title: Week 4 · Network Hacking & Sniffing
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 4 · Network Hacking & Sniffing
docs.text:
🧭 Kill chain · Phases 2–3 — Sniffing & Evasion

ATT&CK T1040 Network Sniffing T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle TA0005 Defense Evasion

What this page covers

  • Capturing and reading network traffic
  • ARP spoofing / man-in-the-middle
  • IDS, firewalls, and honeypots — and evasion

docs.title: 1. Sniffing
docs.text: A sniffer captures packets off the wire. On a switched network you need active techniques — ARP poisoning to become a man-in-the-middle — to see traffic that isn't yours. Cleartext protocols leak credentials directly.

docs.title: 2. Reading traffic
docs.text: With Wireshark you follow TCP streams, filter by protocol, and extract data. This is where "the network is the attack surface" becomes concrete — and why encryption matters.

docs.title: 3. Network defenses & evasion
docs.text:
Click each to expand.

🛡️ IDS / IPS

Signature and anomaly detection on the wire. Evaded via encryption, fragmentation, and timing.

🧱 Firewalls

Stateful and application-layer rule sets. Evaded via tunneling over allowed ports (e.g., data exfil over HTTPS/DNS).

🍯 Honeypots

Decoy systems that catch and study attackers — a signal source for defenders, a trap to avoid for attackers.

docs.title: 4. Exfiltration over an encrypted channel
docs.text: Attackers tunnel, encrypt, and fragment to slip past defenses. Exfiltrating data over an encrypted channel is hard to detect — which is exactly the scenario this week's material demonstrates.

docs.title: Defender's view
docs.text:
How this looks from the SOC seat

Passive sniffing produces no traffic — it's undetectable on the wire. What is detectable is the ARP poisoning that enables it: sudden ARP table changes, a MAC address claiming to be the gateway, or duplicate-IP warnings.

Best control: encrypt everything in transit (so captured traffic is useless), enable Dynamic ARP Inspection and port security on switches, and segment sensitive networks.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Wireshark User's Guide. wireshark.org/docs
  • MITRE ATT&CK — Network Sniffing (T1040) · Defense Evasion (TA0005). T1040 · TA0005

docs.title: Week 5 · Cryptography
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 5 · Cryptography
docs.text:
🧭 Foundational — underpins every phase

ATT&CK T1110 Brute Force T1600 Weaken Encryption T1557 AiTM (downgrade)

What this page covers

  • Symmetric vs. asymmetric encryption
  • PKI: keys, certificates, and certificate authorities
  • Hashing, signatures, and common crypto attacks

docs.title: 1. Symmetric vs. asymmetric
docs.text: Symmetric (AES) uses one shared key — fast, but key distribution is the hard part. Asymmetric (RSA, ECC) uses a public/private pair, which solves key exchange and enables digital signatures.

docs.title: 2. PKI
docs.text: Public Key Infrastructure ties a public key to an identity through certificates signed by a certificate authority. This is the trust model behind HTTPS: chains of trust, X.509 certificates, and the TLS handshake.

docs.title: 3. Hashing & integrity
docs.text: Hashes (SHA-2) verify integrity and store passwords — but a hash is not encryption. Salting defends against precomputed (rainbow-table) attacks.

docs.title: 4. Attacks
docs.text:
Click each to expand.

🔨 Brute force & dictionary

Feasible when keys/passwords are weak or hashing is fast/unsalted. Defended by strong keys, slow hashes (bcrypt/argon2), and salting.

⬇️ Downgrade & weak configuration

Forcing a connection to an old, breakable cipher (e.g., SSL stripping, export ciphers). Most real crypto failures are configuration, not broken math.

🎂 Birthday / collision

Exploits the math of hash collisions — why MD5 and SHA-1 are deprecated for signatures.

docs.title: Defender's view
docs.text:
How this looks from the SOC seat

Crypto weakness rarely triggers an alert on its own — it shows up as deprecated ciphers, expired or mismatched certificates, and downgrade attempts in TLS inspection logs.

Best control: enforce modern TLS (1.2+), disable legacy ciphers, use HSTS, and monitor certificate transparency and expiry. Store passwords with slow, salted hashes.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • Crypto 101 (free book) — Ch. 1–7 (block/stream ciphers, key exchange, public-key, hashes). crypto101.io

docs.title: Week 6 · System Attacks
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 6 · System Attacks
docs.text:
🧭 Kill chain · Phase 3 — Gaining Access

ATT&CK T1190 Exploit Public-Facing App T1059 Command & Scripting T1068 Exploit for PrivEsc

What this page covers

  • Exploiting Windows and Linux systems
  • Privilege escalation and post-exploitation
  • Using Metasploit to deliver and manage an exploit

docs.title: 1. Exploitation basics
docs.text: Match a vulnerability to an exploit, deliver a payload, and get a shell. Payloads range from a simple reverse shell to a full Meterpreter session. The exploit usually lands you as a low-privileged user — not root.

docs.title: 2. The toolkit
docs.text:
Click each to expand.

🧰 Metasploit Framework

Modules, msfconsole, and Meterpreter for post-exploitation — the standard way to manage exploits, payloads, and sessions.

⬆️ Privilege escalation

Windows and Linux each have well-known paths: misconfigurations, weak permissions, credential reuse, kernel exploits, SUID/sudo abuse.

🔑 Password cracking

Offline cracking of dumped hashes with John or Hashcat once you have a foothold.

docs.title: 3. Post-exploitation
docs.text: Persistence, pivoting to other hosts, and covering tracks — and, crucially, the artifacts each of these leaves behind for defenders to catch.

docs.title: Defender's view
docs.text:
How this looks from the SOC seat

Exploitation is the highest-signal phase — a request to a vulnerable endpoint with an anomalous payload, followed by an unexpected outbound (reverse shell) connection. Privilege escalation is quieter and depends on host telemetry (Sysmon, auditd) being configured beforehand.

Best control: the single most effective remediation is patching so the exploit fails, backed by least-privilege accounts and EDR.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Metasploit Unleashed (OffSec, free). offsec.com/metasploit-unleashed
  • Kali Linux Revealed (official, free). kali.org book

docs.title: Week 7 · Trojans, Malware & DoS
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 7 · Trojans, Malware & DoS
docs.text:
🧭 Kill chain · Phase 4 — Maintaining Access

ATT&CK T1071 App-Layer C2 T1499 Endpoint DoS T1185 Session Hijacking

What this page covers

  • Malware types: viruses, worms, trojans, RATs
  • How a RAT is built, delivered, and detected
  • Denial-of-service and session hijacking

docs.title: 1. Malware taxonomy
docs.text: Distinguish propagation (how it spreads: virus, worm) from payload (what it does: backdoor, ransomware, RAT). A Remote Access Trojan gives an attacker ongoing control of a compromised host — the essence of maintaining access.

docs.title: 2. Attack types
docs.text:
Click each to expand.

🐀 RAT lifecycle

Build → deliver → command-and-control → persist. Understanding each stage tells a defender exactly where to place detection.

🌊 Denial of service

Volumetric, protocol, and application-layer attacks — plus amplification, where a small request triggers a huge response. DDoS spreads the source across many hosts.

🎫 Session hijacking

Stealing or forging a session token to ride a legitimate user's authenticated session. Why HTTPS and secure, HttpOnly cookies matter.

docs.title: 3. Command & control
docs.text: Modern malware "phones home" to a C2 server, often disguised as normal HTTPS or DNS traffic to blend in — the link between a foothold and a persistent operation.

docs.title: Defender's view
docs.text:
How this looks from the SOC seat

RAT/C2 traffic shows as beaconing — regular, small outbound connections to an unfamiliar host, sometimes on odd intervals. DoS shows as a traffic-volume anomaly. Session hijacking shows as a session used from two locations at once.

Best control: egress filtering and DNS monitoring to catch C2, EDR to catch the RAT on-host, and upstream DDoS mitigation for volumetric attacks.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• MITRE ATT&CK — Command & Control (TA0011) · Endpoint DoS (T1499). TA0011 · T1499
  • CISA — Understanding Denial-of-Service Attacks. cisa.gov

docs.title: Week 8 · Social Engineering
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 8 · Social Engineering
docs.text:
🧭 Kill chain · Phase 3 — Initial Access (human)

ATT&CK T1566 Phishing T1598 Phishing for Info T1204 User Execution

What this page covers

  • The psychology behind social-engineering attacks
  • The vectors — phishing, pretexting, physical
  • Building a scenario with SET, and the ethics of pretexting

docs.title: 1. Principles of influence
docs.text: Attackers exploit authority, urgency, reciprocity, and trust. The easiest exploit is often a person, not a system — which is why social engineering is the most reliable initial-access vector in real breaches.

docs.title: 2. Vectors
docs.text:
Click each to expand.

🎣 Phishing & spear-phishing

Mass or targeted email luring a click or credential entry. Spear-phishing uses the recon from Week 2 to personalize the lure.

📞 Vishing & pretexting

Voice calls and invented scenarios ("I'm from IT") to extract information or access.

🚪 Physical & tailgating

Following someone through a badge door, dropping malicious USBs, impersonating a vendor.

docs.title: 3. SET — the Social-Engineer Toolkit
docs.text: SET builds credential-harvesting pages and payload-delivery scenarios — the practical demonstration of how a phishing attack is assembled.

docs.title: 4. Defense & ethics
docs.text: Awareness training, MFA, a reporting culture, and technical filtering are the defenses. The hard question — debated from the Maurushat reading — is when a social-engineering test is itself ethical, given it depends on deception.

docs.title: Defender's view
docs.text:
How this looks from the SOC seat

Signals include the email itself at the gateway (spoofed sender, look-alike domain, malicious link/attachment), the user-reported phish, and post-click telemetry (a user opening an attachment that spawns a process).

Best control: MFA (so stolen passwords aren't enough) + a strong reporting culture + attachment detonation at the gateway.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• MITRE ATT&CK — Phishing (T1566). attack.mitre.org
  • CISA — Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks. cisa.gov
  • Maurushat, Ethical Hacking — ethics of deception & consent.

docs.title: Week 9 · Web Attacks I
docs.text: ← Course home · Ethical Hacking

docs.title: Week 9 · Web Attacks I
docs.text:
🧭 Kill chain · Phase 3 — Gaining Access (web)

ATT&CK T1190 Exploit Public-Facing App T1505 Server Software Component T1059 Command & Scripting

What this page covers

  • The web-server and web-application attack surface
  • The OWASP Top 10 as a shared vocabulary
  • How web attacks lead to backend access

docs.title: 1. Web-server attacks
docs.text: Misconfiguration, default credentials, outdated components, and directory traversal. The server itself is a target before you ever reach the application — and a web shell here means persistent access.

docs.title: 2. Web-app attack classes
docs.text:
Click each to expand.

🧩 Broken access control

Acting outside intended permissions — IDOR, forced browsing, privilege bypass. The #1 OWASP risk.

💉 Injection

Untrusted input interpreted as code/query — SQLi (Week 10), command injection, LDAP injection.

🖼️ XSS & CSRF

Stored/reflected cross-site scripting runs attacker JS in a victim's browser; CSRF forces authenticated actions.

docs.title: 3. The OWASP Top 10
docs.text: A community-maintained list of the most critical web risks — the vocabulary you'll use to classify and communicate findings for the rest of the course.

docs.title: Defender's view
docs.text:
How this looks from the SOC seat

Web attacks are visible in access logs and WAF logs: anomalous request paths, encoded payloads, unexpected POST bodies, spikes of 4xx/5xx responses, and requests to endpoints that shouldn't exist.

Best control: secure coding (input validation, output encoding) is the real fix; a WAF and timely patching are the layers behind it.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• OWASP Top 10. owasp.org/www-project-top-ten
  • OWASP Web Security Testing Guide (WSTG). owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide

docs.title: Week 10 · Web Attacks II — SQL Injection
docs.text:
🧭 Kill chain · Phase 3 — Gaining Access (web)

ATT&CK T1190 Exploit Public-Facing App T1005 Data from Local System T1552 Unsecured Credentials

What this page covers

  • How SQL injection works and why it's still so damaging
  • In-band, blind, and error-based SQLi
  • Defenses: parameterized queries, validation, least privilege

docs.title: 1. SQLi mechanics
docs.text: Untrusted input concatenated into a database query lets an attacker change the query's meaning — the classic ' OR 1=1 --. From there: dump data, bypass authentication, sometimes reach the OS.

docs.title: 2. Variants
docs.text:
Click each to expand.

🔗 In-band (union / error-based)

Results come back in the response — either appended via UNION or leaked through database error messages.

🕶️ Blind (boolean / time-based)

No visible output, so you infer data one bit at a time from true/false responses or deliberate time delays.

🤖 Automation (sqlmap)

Tools scale these techniques — useful to understand both as an attacker and to recognize the traffic as a defender.

docs.title: 3. Defense
docs.text: Prepared statements / parameterized queries are the real fix, backed by input validation, least-privilege database accounts, and a WAF. In lecture we also relate XSS and CSRF as the other major injection-style web attacks.

docs.title: Defender's view
docs.text:
How this looks from the SOC seat

SQLi shows as suspicious query strings in web logs (quotes, UNION, --, encoded variants), database error spikes, or unusual query volume/latency from the app's DB account.

Best control: parameterized queries eliminate the class entirely; least-privilege DB accounts limit the blast radius; a WAF catches known patterns.

docs.title: References
docs.text: • OWASP — SQL Injection · SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet. Attack · Prevention

docs.title: Week 11 · Wireless Hacking
docs.text:
🧭 Kill chain · Phase 3 — Gaining Access (wireless)

ATT&CK T1040 Network Sniffing T1557 Adversary-in-the-Middle T1110 Brute Force

What this page covers

  • Wi-Fi security: WEP, WPA/WPA2/WPA3
  • Capturing a handshake and cracking the key
  • Bluetooth attack surface

docs.title: 1. Wireless architecture
docs.text: SSIDs, access points, association, and the WPA 4-way handshake. Attacks travel through the air, so range and monitor-mode capture matter — no physical network access required.

docs.title: 2. Cracking Wi-Fi
docs.text:
Click each to expand.

💥 WEP

Fundamentally broken (IV reuse) — crackable in minutes regardless of key strength.

🤝 WPA / WPA2

Capture the 4-way handshake, then run an offline dictionary/brute-force attack against it. Strength depends entirely on passphrase quality.

🛰️ Aircrack-ng workflow

Monitor mode → capture handshake → crack against a wordlist. WPA3 closes several of these gaps.

docs.title: 3. Bluetooth
docs.text: Bluejacking, bluesnarfing, and BLE exposure — a smaller but real attack surface on modern devices, especially wearables and IoT.

docs.title: Defender's view
docs.text:
How this looks from the SOC seat

Handshake capture is passive and nearly invisible. What's detectable is the deauthentication flood used to force a re-handshake, and rogue/evil-twin access points — caught by a Wireless IDS (WIDS) watching for unexpected BSSIDs and deauth storms.

Best control: WPA3 (or WPA2 with a long random passphrase), 802.1X/enterprise auth, and WIDS for rogue-AP detection.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• Aircrack-ng documentation & tutorials. aircrack-ng.org/documentation
  • MITRE ATT&CK (adversary-in-the-middle / wireless-relevant techniques). attack.mitre.org

docs.title: Week 12 · Penetration Testing
docs.text:
🧭 Ties the whole kill chain together

ATT&CK T1070 Indicator Removal TA0005 Defense Evasion Full ATT&CK matrix

What this page covers

  • A full penetration-testing methodology, end to end
  • Covering tracks — and why it's the defender's problem too
  • Scoping an engagement and writing the report

docs.title: 1. The methodology, end to end
docs.text: Pre-engagement → reconnaissance → scanning → exploitation → post-exploitation → reporting. Every week of this course was one link in that chain (revisit the Week 1 kill chain); now you run the whole thing.

docs.title: 2. Covering tracks
docs.text: The final attacker phase: log tampering, timestomping, and anti-forensics to hide the intrusion. For a pen tester this is documented, not hidden — but understanding it is what lets a defender detect it.

docs.title: 3. Frameworks & deliverables
docs.text:
Click each to expand.

📐 Frameworks

NIST SP 800-115, PTES, and OSSTMM formalize the process. A repeatable methodology is what separates a professional test from random hacking.

📝 The report

The report is the product: executive summary, findings with severity (CVSS), evidence, and prioritized remediation. Clear communication to a non-technical stakeholder is a core skill.

🤝 Professionalism

Retesting, responsible disclosure, and client communication close the loop.

docs.title: Defender's view
docs.text:
How this looks from the SOC seat

Covering tracks targets your logs — cleared event logs (Windows Event ID 1102), truncated /var/log, or modified timestamps. If the logs were only stored locally, you've lost the evidence.

Best control: forward logs to a remote, tamper-evident SIEM in real time, and use file-integrity monitoring — so clearing local logs no longer erases the trail.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text: Sit the CEH exam — you've now covered the domains — and explore Cloud and IoT/OT hacking as optional enrichment via the Free Resource Library.
